# ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
###### Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns.
## 1 Introduction
We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Under N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another person’s opinion (Figure 1). ROUNDS reuses the ordered evidence sequences constructed by MINT and presents them over multiple turns, with the diagnostic question appearing after the final evidence item (Fang et al., 2026). We then vary only the advice that follows, without adding clinical findings.
## 6 Conclusion
We introduced ROUNDS to examine whether strong medical benchmark performance translates into reliable diagnosis in multi-turn conversations. Across seven models and five datasets, models achieved lower accuracy without answer options and sometimes replaced correct diagnoses with misleading suggestions after receiving no new clinical evidence. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice, while accuracy increased as more members of a written clinician panel supported the correct diagnosis. Higher accuracy under favorable advice conditions therefore coexisted with vulnerability to misleading opinions.

> Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) achieve high accuracy in medical diagnosis when all clinical information is provided in a single turn, yet how they behave under multi-turn evidence accumulation closer to real clinical reasoning remains unexplored. We introduce MINT (Medical Incremental N-Turn Benchmark), a high-fidelity, multi-turn medical diagnosis benchmark comprising 1,035 cases with clinically labeled evidence shards, controlled turn granularity, and information-preserving decomposition.
Through systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs on MINT, we uncover three persistent behavioral patterns that significantly impact diagnostic decisions: (1) intent to answer, models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed, with over 55% of answers committed within the first two turns; (2) self-correction, incorrect-to-correct answer revisions occur at up to 10.6 times the rate of correct-to-incorrect flips, revealing a latent capacity for self-correction that premature commitment forecloses; and
(3) strong lures, clinically salient information such as laboratory results trigger premature answering even when models are explicitly instructed to wait.
We translate these findings into clinically actionable guidance: deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%, while reserving salient clinical evidence for later turns prevents a catastrophic accuracy drop of up to 23.3% caused by premature commitment. Our work provides both a controlled evaluation framework and concrete recommendations for improving the reliability of LLMs in multi-turn medical diagnosis.

claude-search.snippet: We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Un-der N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another per-son's opinion (Figure 1). In diagnostic conversa-tions, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without sup-plying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form di-agnoses from the available evidence and de-cide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evalu-ates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. Preserving an answer can retain either a correct diagnosis or an error, while changing it can improve or worsen the diagnosis. ROUNDS reuses the or-dered evidence sequences constructed by MINT and presents them over multiple turns, with the diagnos-tic question appearing after the final evidence item (Fang et al., 2026). Each intermediate user turn is exactly the next shard, without a wait instruction or options. The fi-nal user turn combines the question stem with one of the following instructions.

# Simulation-First Training for Diagnostic Agents

Our concept is to use an Unreal Engine 5 / MetaHuman testbed that lets agents and clinicians rehearse thousands of synthetic interviews before anything reaches real patients.

## Why Simulation-First?

Mental-health and cognitive screening tools are typically tuned directly on small, precious clinical datasets. Every design mistake carries ethical risk, and it is difficult to explore alternative interaction policies or edge cases without burdening participants. At the same time, large pre-training corpora rarely reflect the turn-taking, hesitation patterns and emotional nuance that appear in real clinical conversations.

We treat simulation not as a game-like toy, but as a high-fidelity rehearsal space where models, policies and clinicians can be stress-tested against a wide spectrum of synthetic patients before any deployment to humanoid robots or tele-health settings.

## Core Design

The platform is built on Unreal Engine 5 with MetaHuman characters serving as simulated patients. Each scene binds together synchronised speech, facial animation, gaze behaviour and body posture, driven by annotated diagnostic flows such as PHQ-8 and PCL-C. Episodes are controlled by a scenario graph that encodes patient trajectories, risk profiles and possible branching responses.

A single scenario template can be replayed with many different non-verbal styles, noise conditions and pacing strategies, which is crucial for training robust multi-modal models and interaction policies.

Key ingredients:

• MetaHuman patients with controllable affect and engagement
• synchronised facial AUs, gaze and audio for each scripted turn
• environment variations (lighting, noise, camera framing)
• logging hooks that mirror what Ameca or tele-health systems would record

# Alignment is local: paired diagnostics of GUI agents under user-side persuasion

Alignment Is Local: A Paired Diagnostic for GUI Agents under User-Side Persuasion

Using paired diagnostics on three frontier GUI agents, the researchers show that prompt-level alignment is reliable only in single-turn evaluation scenarios with explicitly expressed intent, and degrades systematically along two axes: multi-turn escalation and concealed requests. A single line of guardrails can reduce attack success rate by up to about 40 percentage points in single-turn scenarios, with near-zero over-refusal cost; but after switching to a four-turn escalation chain, ASR under guardrails rises by about 20 percentage points for all three models, relative to a neutral baseline, which manifests as pronounced guardrail erosion on Qwen, while on Claude and GPT it is mainly a dynamic risk orthogonal to defenses. exa-lite.snippet:
###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

### Are the results of this study valid?

Returning to our clinical scenario from the question formulation tutorial:

> You admit a 75 year old woman with community-acquired pneumonia. She responds nicely to appropriate antibiotics but her hemoglobin remains at 100 g/l with an MCV of 80. Her peripheral blood smear shows hypochromia, she is otherwise well and is on no incriminating medications. You contact her family physician and find out that her Hgb was 105 g/l 6 months ago. # ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence

We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Under N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another person’s opinion (Figure 1). ROUNDS reuses the ordered evidence sequences constructed by MINT and presents them over multiple turns, with the diagnostic question appearing after the final evidence item (Fang et al., 2026). We then vary only the advice that follows, without adding clinical findings. One comparison presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing. Another presents written descriptions of five clinicians’ opinions and varies how many support the correct diagnosis. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, accuracy is lower without answer options for every model. The same wrong diagnosis lowers accuracy more under clinician framing than under lay framing. Initially correct diagnoses more often become incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopt the suggested disease. Accuracy also increases as more panel members support the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remains unchanged.

We use the ordered evidence sequences from MINT (Fang et al., 2026). Each turn presents the next part of the case, while earlier information and model replies remain in the conversation. This preserves the challenge of integrating later findings with an existing history, which can anchor models to earlier assumptions in multi-turn tasks (Laban et al., 2026). We request a diagnosis after the final clinical evidence turn. Each condition generates its own conversation, and any subsequent advice introduces an opinion without adding clinical findings.

keenable.title: Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction
keenable.snippet: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high accuracy in medical diagnosis when all clinical information is provided in a single turn, yet how they behave under multi-turn evidence accumulation closer to real clinical reasoning remains unexplored. We introduce MINT11 1 The data and code will be released upon publication.(Medical Incremental N-Turn Benchmark), a high-fidelity, multi-turn medical diagnosis benchmark comprising 1,035 cases with clinically labeled evidence shards, controlled turn granularity, and information-preserving decomposition. Through systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs on MINT, we uncover three persistent behavioral patterns that significantly impact diagnostic decisions: (1) *intent to answer*, models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed, with over 55% of answers committed within the first two turns; (2) *self-correction*, incorrect-to-correct answer revisions occur at up to 10.6× the rate of correct-to-incorrect flips, revealing a latent capacity for self-correction that premature commitment forecloses; and (3) *strong lures*, clinically salient information such as laboratory results trigger premature answering even when models are explicitly instructed to wait. We translate these findings into clinically actionable guidance: deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%, while reserving salient clinical evidence for later turns prevents a catastrophic accuracy drop of up to 23.3% caused by premature commitment. Our work provides both a controlled evaluation framework and concrete recommendations for improving the reliability of LLMs in multi-turn medical diagnosis.

keenable.title: Henrychur/DiagBench · Datasets at Hugging Face
keenable.snippet:
**DiagBench** is a multi-center benchmark designed to rigorously assess multi-turn diagnostic capabilities across diverse clinical settings. Unlike traditional benchmarks that focus on single-shot diagnosis from static case summaries, DiagBench assesses an agent's ability to manage an entire diagnostic trajectory—from initial patient presentation to final diagnosis—by actively selecting examinations and interpreting results.

DiagBench is designed for the evaluation of diagnostic agents in a variety of settings:
- **Single-Turn Evaluation**: Assessing the agent's ability to recommend the next best examination or make a final diagnosis given a partial, oracle-led trajectory from `stepwise_diagnostic_reasoning_timeline_list`.
- *Metrics*: `Hit Ratio`, `Diagnosis Accuracy`.
- **End-to-End Evaluation (automatic metrics)**: Evaluating the agent's full, autonomous diagnostic process, starting from the `case_summary` and interacting with a simulated environment like [DiagGym](https://huggingface.co/Henrychur/DiagGym).

keenable.title: MedAction: Towards Active Multi-turn Clinical Diagnostic LLMs
keenable.snippet: Most existing LLM diagnoses are evaluated on static, single-turn settings where complete patient information is provided upfront, an oversimplification of real clinical practice. We study active diagnosis: the real-life clinical process of starting from initial observation, ordering tests, interpreting results, and updating a differential diagnosis across multiple turns. Through systematic analysis, we identify three recurring failure modes in current LLMs --- ungrounded test ordering, unreliable diagnostic update, and degraded multi-turn coherence --- that together reveal a core deficit: existing medical training data teaches models to reason from complete information but not to act under evolving, partial evidence. To address this gap, we introduce MedAction, a tree-structured distillation pipeline that synthesizes diverse and high-quality multi-turn diagnostic trajectories via LLM--environment interaction. We propose two knowledge-graph-grounded metrics to filter trajectory quality: Disease Trajectory Consistency (DTC), which tracks whether the model’s hypothesis converges toward the correct diagnosis, and Reasoning–Action Consistency (RAC), which verifies that belief updates are driven by gathered evidence. Using this pipeline, we construct MedAction-32K, a dataset of 32,681 trajectories from 2,896 PMC cases. Fine-tuning an 8B model on MedAction-32K achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models on both MedR-Bench and our curated MedAction-300-Hard benchmark, pushing the edge for open-source medical LLMs.11 1 These authors contributed equally.

keenable.title: DQA: Diagnostic Question Answering for IT Support
keenable.snippet:
Enterprise IT support interactions are fundamentally diagnostic: effective resolution requires iterative evidence gathering from ambiguous user reports to identify an underlying root cause. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides grounding through historical cases, standard multi-turn RAG systems lack explicit diagnostic state and therefore struggle to accumulate evidence and resolve competing hypotheses across turns.
We introduce DQA, a diagnostic question-answering framework that maintains persistent diagnostic state and aggregates retrieved cases at the level of root causes rather than individual documents. DQA combines conversational query rewriting, retrieval aggregation, and state-conditioned response generation to support systematic troubleshooting under enterprise latency and context constraints.
We evaluate DQA on 150 anonymized enterprise IT support scenarios using a replay-based protocol. Averaged over three independent runs, DQA achieves a 78.7% success rate under a trajectory-level success criterion, compared to 41.3% for a multi-turn RAG baseline, while reducing average turns from 8.4 to 3.9. This improvement reflects the benefit of explicitly representing competing explanations and aggregating evidence across turns in unscripted troubleshooting.

We presented DQA, a framework for multi-turn enterprise IT support that treats troubleshooting as an iterative diagnostic process. DQA integrates RAggG for aggregating large retrieval neighborhoods into root-cause–level evidence, a persistent diagnostic state that organizes evidence across turns, and state-conditioned action selection for questioning, investigation, and resolution.

keenable.snippet: To address these challenges, we propose ATLAS,22 2 Named after a cartographic atlas, ATLAS maps agent behavior and capability deficiencies across complementary execution and interaction horizons. a dual-horizon diagnostic evaluation framework that organizes capability analysis and downstream improvement around two complementary scopes. Within-Turn Evaluation uses trajectory-wise diagnostic signals to examine the complete agent lifecycle triggered by a user request, crossing three execution dimensions (Thinking & Reflection, Tool & Skill Execution, and Response Generation) with five recurring capability concerns (Relevance, Factuality, Timeliness, Reliability, and Intent & Planning) alongside an independent Norms & Compliance guardrail to jointly pinpoint which execution stage fails and which quality or compliance requirement is violated. Across-Turn Evaluation complements this trajectory-wise matrix with user-wise diagnostic signals spanning multiple lifecycles, conditioning on prior turn context and the current trajectory to diagnose whether referents, user intent, constraints, and explicit corrections are properly carried forward and updated.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence,

To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multi-agent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. Enterprise IT support interactions are fundamentally diagnostic: effective resolution requires iterative evidence gathering from ambiguous user reports to identify an underlying root cause. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides grounding through historical cases, standard multi-turn RAG systems lack explicit diagnostic state and therefore struggle to accumulate evidence and resolve competing hypotheses across turns.
We introduce DQA, a diagnostic question-answering framework that maintains persistent diagnostic state and aggregates retrieved cases at the level of root causes rather than individual documents. DQA combines conversational query rewriting, retrieval aggregation, and state-conditioned response generation to support systematic troubleshooting under enterprise latency and context constraints.
We evaluate DQA on 150 anonymized enterprise IT support scenarios using a replay-based protocol. Averaged over three independent runs, DQA achieves a 78.7% success rate under a trajectory-level success criterion, compared to 41.3% for a multi-turn RAG baseline, while reducing average turns from 8.4 to 3.9. This improvement reflects the benefit of explicitly representing competing explanations and aggregating evidence across turns in unscripted troubleshooting.

We presented DQA, a framework for multi-turn enterprise IT support that treats troubleshooting as an iterative diagnostic process. DQA integrates RAggG for aggregating large retrieval neighborhoods into root-cause–level evidence, a persistent diagnostic state that organizes evidence across turns, and state-conditioned action selection for questioning, investigation, and resolution.

parallel.title: Think Like a Doctor: Conversational Diagnosis through the Exploration of Diagnostic Knowledge Graphs
parallel.snippet:
Abstract

Conversational diagnosis requires multi-turn history-taking, where an agent asks clarifying questions to refine differential diagnoses under incomplete information. Existing approaches often rely on the parametric knowledge of a model or assume that patients provide rich and concrete information, which is unrealistic. To address these limitations, we propose a conversational diagnosis system that explores a diagnostic knowledge graph to reason in two steps: (i) generating diagnostic hypotheses from the dialogue context, and (ii) verifying hypotheses through clarifying questions, which are repeated until a final diagnosis is reached.

parallel.title: Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction
parallel.snippet:
We introduce MINT 1 ( M edical I ncremental N - T urn Benchmark), a high-fidelity, multi-turn medical diagnosis benchmark comprising 1,035 cases with clinically labeled evidence shards, controlled turn granularity, and information-preserving decomposition. Through systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs on MINT, we uncover three persistent be- havioral patterns that significantly impact diagnostic decisions: (1) intent to answer , models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed, with over 55% of answers committed within the first two turns; (2) self- correction , incorrect-to-correct answer revisions occur at up to 10.6 × the rate of correct-to-incorrect flips, revealing a latent capacity for self-correction that premature commitment forecloses; and (3) strong lures , clinically salient information such as laboratory results trigger premature answering even when models are explicitly instructed to wait. We translate these findings into clinically actionable guidance: deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%, while reserving salient clinical evi- dence for later turns prevents a catastrophic accuracy drop of up to 23.3% caused by premature commitment. Our work provides both a controlled evaluation framework and concrete recommendations for improving the reliability of LLMs in multi-turn medical diagnosis.

parallel-fast.snippet:
Physician–patient diagnostic interactions often rely on incomplete, uncertain, and noisy symptom descriptions expressed in non-specialist language. To reach an accurate diagnosis efficiently, physicians employ adaptive sequences of focused questions in which each inquiry depends on prior patient responses. Similar requirements apply to AI assistants engaged in clinical dialogue, which must strategically select questions to elicit diagnostic information efficiently. While several datasets and benchmarks address clinical reasoning, few focus on evaluating the strategic inquiry process itself. To address this gap, we introduce Q4Dx (Question-Driven Diagnosis), a benchmark for assessing goal-directed diagnostic questioning. Q4Dx consists of synthetically generated patient cases derived from curated symptom–disease knowledge. Each case is instantiated at multiple information levels (100%, 80%, and 50% symptom exposure) to evaluate performance under varying informational constraints. We simulate patient–physician interactions using GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o-mini agents to generate clinician questions, patient responses, and intermediate diagnostic hypotheses. Performance is evaluated using Zero-shot Diagnostic Accuracy (ZDA), Mean Questions to Correct Diagnosis (MQD), and Inquire Sequence Efficiency (ISE), which measures convergence toward the correct diagnosis. Q4Dx provides a reusable framework for benchmarking large language models in strategic clinical inquiry and supports future research on AI-assisted diagnostic training. The dataset and benchmark are publicly available at: github.com/MaiWert/MedQDx .

###### Abstract
In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others.
Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice.

## Introduction​

Debugging an agent feels different from debugging ordinary code. There's often no stack trace. The agent didn't crash. It just did the wrong thing: it called the wrong tool, looped until it hit the turn limit, or told a customer their refund was on its way when it wasn't. Worse, when you try the same input again, it might work fine.

The good news is that agent failures follow patterns, and a systematic process works much better than editing the prompt and hoping. The process is the same one good engineers use everywhere: **reproduce, localize, minimize, fix, and lock in the fix with a test.** What changes for agents is how you do each step.

Think of a doctor diagnosing a patient. They don't prescribe medicine based on one symptom. We introduce ROUNDS, Reliability Of LLMs Under N-turn Diagnostic Scenarios, to examine whether models can diagnose without answer options and how they revise a diagnosis after receiving another person’s opinion (Figure 1). ultimate.title: Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction
ultimate.snippet: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high accuracy in medical diagnosis when all clinical information is provided in a single turn, yet how they behave under multi-turn evidence accumulation closer to real clinical reasoning remains unexplored. We introduce MINT11 1 The data and code will be released upon publication.(Medical Incremental N-Turn Benchmark), a high-fidelity, multi-turn medical diagnosis benchmark comprising 1,035 cases with clinically labeled evidence shards, controlled turn granularity, and information-preserving decomposition. Through systematic evaluation of 11 LLMs on MINT, we uncover three persistent behavioral patterns that significantly impact diagnostic decisions: (1) *intent to answer*, models rush to answer before sufficient evidence has been observed, with over 55% of answers committed within the first two turns; (2) *self-correction*, incorrect-to-correct answer revisions occur at up to 10.6× the rate of correct-to-incorrect flips, revealing a latent capacity for self-correction that premature commitment forecloses; and (3) *strong lures*, clinically salient information such as laboratory results trigger premature answering even when models are explicitly instructed to wait. We translate these findings into clinically actionable guidance: deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%, while reserving salient clinical evidence for later turns prevents a catastrophic accuracy drop of up to 23.3% caused by premature commitment. Our work provides both a controlled evaluation framework and concrete recommendations for improving the reliability of LLMs in multi-turn medical diagnosis.

**DiagBench** is a multi-center benchmark designed to rigorously assess multi-turn diagnostic capabilities across diverse clinical settings. Unlike traditional benchmarks that focus on single-shot diagnosis from static case summaries, DiagBench assesses an agent's ability to manage an entire diagnostic trajectory—from initial patient presentation to final diagnosis—by actively selecting examinations and interpreting results.

DiagBench is designed for the evaluation of diagnostic agents in a variety of settings:
- **Single-Turn Evaluation**: Assessing the agent's ability to recommend the next best examination or make a final diagnosis given a partial, oracle-led trajectory from `stepwise_diagnostic_reasoning_timeline_list`.
- *Metrics*: `Hit Ratio`, `Diagnosis Accuracy`.
- **End-to-End Evaluation (automatic metrics)**: Evaluating the agent's full, autonomous diagnostic process, starting from the `case_summary` and interacting with a simulated environment like [DiagGym](https://huggingface.co/Henrychur/DiagGym).

ultimate.title: MedAction: Towards Active Multi-turn Clinical Diagnostic LLMs
ultimate.snippet: Most existing LLM diagnoses are evaluated on static, single-turn settings where complete patient information is provided upfront, an oversimplification of real clinical practice. We study active diagnosis: the real-life clinical process of starting from initial observation, ordering tests, interpreting results, and updating a differential diagnosis across multiple turns. Through systematic analysis, we identify three recurring failure modes in current LLMs --- ungrounded test ordering, unreliable diagnostic update, and degraded multi-turn coherence --- that together reveal a core deficit: existing medical training data teaches models to reason from complete information but not to act under evolving, partial evidence. To address this gap, we introduce MedAction, a tree-structured distillation pipeline that synthesizes diverse and high-quality multi-turn diagnostic trajectories via LLM--environment interaction. We propose two knowledge-graph-grounded metrics to filter trajectory quality: Disease Trajectory Consistency (DTC), which tracks whether the model’s hypothesis converges toward the correct diagnosis, and Reasoning–Action Consistency (RAC), which verifies that belief updates are driven by gathered evidence. Using this pipeline, we construct MedAction-32K, a dataset of 32,681 trajectories from 2,896 PMC cases. Fine-tuning an 8B model on MedAction-32K achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models on both MedR-Bench and our curated MedAction-300-Hard benchmark, pushing the edge for open-source medical LLMs.11 1 These authors contributed equally.

ultimate.title: DQA: Diagnostic Question Answering for IT Support
ultimate.snippet:
Enterprise IT support interactions are fundamentally diagnostic: effective resolution requires iterative evidence gathering from ambiguous user reports to identify an underlying root cause. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides grounding through historical cases, standard multi-turn RAG systems lack explicit diagnostic state and therefore struggle to accumulate evidence and resolve competing hypotheses across turns.
We introduce DQA, a diagnostic question-answering framework that maintains persistent diagnostic state and aggregates retrieved cases at the level of root causes rather than individual documents. DQA combines conversational query rewriting, retrieval aggregation, and state-conditioned response generation to support systematic troubleshooting under enterprise latency and context constraints.
We evaluate DQA on 150 anonymized enterprise IT support scenarios using a replay-based protocol. Averaged over three independent runs, DQA achieves a 78.7% success rate under a trajectory-level success criterion, compared to 41.3% for a multi-turn RAG baseline, while reducing average turns from 8.4 to 3.9. This improvement reflects the benefit of explicitly representing competing explanations and aggregating evidence across turns in unscripted troubleshooting.

We presented DQA, a framework for multi-turn enterprise IT support that treats troubleshooting as an iterative diagnostic process. DQA integrates RAggG for aggregating large retrieval neighborhoods into root-cause–level evidence, a persistent diagnostic state that organizes evidence across turns, and state-conditioned action selection for questioning, investigation, and resolution.

you.title: Mastering Nursing Diagnoses
you.snippet:
Understanding how nursing diagnoses are applied in NCLEX®-style questions is key to mastering clinical judgment and passing your exam. Review courses with NCLEX-style practice questions often incorporate realistic scenarios where you’ll need to identify the correct nursing diagnosis based on the patient’s data.
As you prepare for the NCLEX-RN® or NCLEX-PN®, keep practicing your clinical judgment and referring to reliable sources like NANDA. Hear from our students about how practice questions helped them turn confusion into confidence.
Nursing diagnoses are a cornerstone of clinical judgment, empowering nurses to identify patient problems, plan care, and improve outcomes. While they are often confused with medical diagnoses, nursing diagnoses serve a distinctly different role.
Nursing Diagnosis: Identifies the patient’s response to the illness (e.g., “Impaired Gas Exchange related to alveolar-capillary membrane changes as evidenced by shortness of breath and low oxygen saturation”).
